# Diagnosing a 2011 Ford Fusion SEL: When Power Exists but Crank Signal Fails

You have verified the battery, confirmed all fuses are intact, and observed that the headlights remain bright when attempting to start. Yet, the starter motor refuses to engage, producing no clicks or whirrs. In automotive diagnostics, this specific symptomâfull system voltage with zero crank attemptâis a critical pivot point. It tells you the vehicle's primary power rail is healthy, but the control logic has likely disabled the starter circuit before it can be energized.

The most probable culprit in this scenario is the Powertrain Control Module (PCM) or its internal starter disable relay, often referred to as the "starter inhibit" function. Modern vehicles like the 2011 Fusion SEL rely on the PCM to control the starter solenoid rather than using a purely mechanical ignition switch. If the PCM detects an anomaly during the key-on/ignition sequence, it will intentionally cut power to the starter circuit to protect the engine from uncontrolled cranking or potential damage.

The source material notes that the instrument cluster displays "everything is faulty" while other electronics function normally. This behavior strongly suggests a communication timeout between the PCM and the Engine Control Module (ECM), or a severe software corruption event. When the vehicle's computer reads its own diagnostic trouble codes (DTCs) as invalid during initialization, it often enters a fail-safe mode. In this state, the PCM disables non-critical accessories and, crucially, the starter motor. The fact that the dashboard lights on the floorboard turn off only while the key is in the start position confirms that the ignition switch is sending the correct signal to the vehicle's electronics; however, the PCM is not responding by activating the relay.

To resolve this without immediately replacing expensive modules, you must verify the communication bus integrity. The issue could stem from a blown internal fuse within the PCM itself or a failure in the CAN (Controller Area Network) network that links the PCM to other control units. Since the radio and other accessories work, the main power supply is fine, but the data paths might be disrupted.

A practical first step involves checking the "starter disable" relay location, often found under the dash near the steering column or in the engine bay fuse box, depending on the specific trim level. Even if external fuses appear good, a corroded terminal at the PCM connector can mimic a total system failure. Inspect the pins for green corrosion or loose fitment. If the connectors are clean and secure, the issue likely resides within the software logic of the PCM.

In many cases involving Ford vehicles of this era, a simple reprogramming or reflashing of the Powertrain Control Module restores communication with the ECM and clears the false "faulty" status codes. Before resorting to module replacement, ensure you have access to the specific diagnostic tool capable of writing the correct calibration file for your VIN. If the PCM has suffered internal damage due to a voltage spike (which can happen even if the battery tests good), replacement might be necessary. However, swapping the module without copying the immobilizer keys from the old unit to the new one will leave the car unable to start even after repair, as the engine ECU and transaxle will not allow fuel injection or gear engagement without a valid match.

Once the communication is restored and the PCM responds to the ignition signal, the starter circuit should engage normally. If you still hear no sound, trace the power feed from the relay to the starter solenoid input wire with a multimeter while a helper turns the key. If there is voltage at the starter but no crank, the solenoid or motor internals are mechanically failed. But given the "all systems faulty" readout, fixing the control module logic is the priority.

After resolving the start issue, you can finally address the persistent chime noises by tracing the audio output from the instrument cluster to its source speakers or internal buzzer, likely located behind the dash trim panels.
